title: Celebrating others
hook: Moggallana reads the joy on Sariputta's face before a word is said: mudita, joy at another's joy
tomorrow: why did people call a holy man a glutton?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: savor. Thoreau gave a good morning a broad margin. Today, a good moment that belongs to someone else.

A friend's name lights up the phone: I GOT IT. There's a half-second before typing congrats when anything can happen. Two young friends in the Buddha's time, Sariputta and Moggallana, made a pact: whoever finds the deathless first will tell the other. One morning Sariputta meets a monk named Assaji, walking for alms, so calm that Sariputta has to ask who his teacher is. Assaji gives him a few lines of the Buddha's teaching, and Sariputta understands. He walks back to his friend. And before he says a word, Moggallana sees his face.
screen: `I GOT IT.` → `A PACT BETWEEN FRIENDS.` → `ASSAJI'S FEW LINES.` → `MOGGALLANA SEES HIS FACE.`

segments.voice: In the Vinaya, the monks' book of discipline, Moggallana says, in effect: your face is calm, friend, your skin is bright. Have you found the deathless? He reads the joy on his friend's face and asks about it before Sariputta says a word. No race. No "why him first". Then Sariputta shares the verse, Moggallana understands too, and the two go to the Buddha together. Buddhism has a word for that turn toward a friend's good: mudita, joy at another's joy. It's one of the four boundless states the Buddha taught, beside loving-kindness, compassion and equanimity, and it's practiced on purpose: wishing that another's good fortune will last. It can even be heard: in Theravada Buddhist communities, when someone does a good deed, people around them may say sadhu, sadhu, sadhu: well done, said three times. That's mudita out loud. The teaching under it: someone else's win doesn't subtract from yours. It adds a second joy, if you let it in. Envy shrinks the world to one winner. Mudita makes room for two, and it can be practiced, like any other skill.
screen: `YOUR FACE IS CALM, FRIEND.` · `HE SAW IT BEFORE A WORD.` · `MUDITA: JOY AT ANOTHER'S JOY.` · `SADHU, SADHU, SADHU.` · then, large: `GLAD FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who has good news right now, big or small. Write them a message that's only about their joy: no "me too", no advice, no comparison. Read it once, slowly, and let their good news be good.
Celebrating others: mudita, joy at someone else's joy, one of the four boundless states in Buddhist teaching.
Your line: glad for you. Moggallana saw his friend's joy before a word was said. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Buddhists cultivate mudita, sympathetic joy, as one of the four brahmaviharas, often in meditation that wishes others' good fortune to last; in Theravada communities people may say 'sadhu' three times to rejoice in a good deed.

chat.says: Inés made partner!! so happy for her. also a tiny bit sick about my own job. awful?
options: not awful. mudita gets practiced: turn toward her joy first, and it can grow.
awful. any envy at all means your happiness for her isn't real.
fair. celebrate her later, once your own career has caught up.
chat.meaning: Mudita is joy at another's joy, and Buddhists practice it on purpose. A pang doesn't cancel it; turning toward her joy grows it.
